title: Not doomed: Examining the path from misinformation exposure to verification and correction in the context of COVID-19 pandemic
screen_reason: The study's AIM is a path model from misinformation exposure to verification/correction intentions, which by itself would be excluded. But the sample description reports one descriptive share of respondents above a threshold: 79.26% of the 410 U.S. adults said they OFTEN encountered news and information containing misleading content. Under §1 that is a RECALL (exposure) estimate, and under the 'a study whose aim is something else is still included if a descriptive share is reported anywhere' rule the paper is eligible. Everything else in the paper is scale means or path coefficients.

estimates.platform: online survey (Amazon MTurk); the item is not platform-specific
estimates.measure_type: % of survey respondents who said they often encounter news and information that contain misleading content
estimates.denominator: 410 U.S. adults recruited through Amazon MTurk in May 2021 (448 started; 38 dropped for incomplete or missing critical answers); age 18-75, M = 33.98, 58.29% female, 68.54% Caucasian, 65.12% Bachelor's or above
estimates.definition: respondent indicated they often encountered news and information that contain misleading content (self-report; the exact item wording, scale and 'often' cut-point are not reported)
estimates.misinfo_def: "Often defined as false or inaccurate information, misinformation could inflame social conflicts"
estimates.source_quote: The majority (79.26 %) indicated that they often encountered news and information that contain misleading content.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Single self-report item reported only in the sample description; the respondent is the judge of what counts as misleading. Item wording, response scale and the threshold collapsed into 'often' are not given, so the figure cannot be reconstructed.
estimates.moderator_quote: Data were collected in May 2021 with an online survey conducted via Amazon MTurk. A total of 448 adults participated in the survey; 38 individuals who failed to complete the survey or missed answers to critical questions were excluded. The final sample consisted of 410 individuals ranging in age from 18 to 75 (M = 33.98, SD = 10.79).
estimates.notes: topic coded general_news, not covid19: although the study is framed around COVID-19 and its exposure/misperception scales use COVID-19 claims, THIS item asks generically about 'news and information that contain misleading content' with no topic restriction. Confidence is medium rather than high only because the item's wording and threshold are never given — the value itself is printed verbatim. MTurk is a non-probability opt-in pool, so sampling_frame = convenience despite the author's claim of a 'national and representative participant pool'.

missed_or_uncertain: Seen and deliberately NOT extracted: (1) The three misinformation-exposure scales are reported as MEANS ONLY on a 0-6 'not at all' to 'a lot' scale — social media M = 2.71 (SD 1.63), online news websites M = 1.68 (SD 1.72), interpersonal communication M = 2.29 (SD 1.66) — with no share of respondents above any threshold, so per §1 they yield no rows even though they are the paper's central exposure measure. This is a pity: these are the more precisely measured quantities (frequency of having read each of five specific widely debunked COVID-19 claims, per source), and a share-based version of them would have been the better estimate. (2) Misperceptions scale M = 1.72 (SD 1.71) on 0-6 across eight false COVID-19 claims — belief, explicitly excluded. (3) Path coefficients and bootstrap mediation effects (Table 2, Fig. 2) — effect sizes, not prevalence. (4) Figures cited from OTHER sources and therefore barred by R8: 'more than 10 % of online news sites spread deceptive or inaccurate information' and 'NewsGuard (2019) reported that 11 % of these news sites publish health-related misinformation' (from a NewsGuard report on 3,000 sites); 'misinformation is 70 % more likely to be shared than truthful information on social media' (Vosoughi et al. 2018); 'around 80 % of respondents think misinformation awaits prompt attention' (Mitchell et al. 2019); 'three in four Americans tend to wrongfully overestimate their abilities to distinguish between legitimate news and misinformation' (Lyons et al. 2021); Facebook takedown counts (7 million posts, 98 million warning labels, Lerman 2020). None of these are this paper's own data.

rob.design: Cross-sectional online survey of U.S. adults via Amazon MTurk, May 2021. 448 recruited, 410 analysed after excluding 38 incomplete/critical-missing (retention 91.5%); no response rate is calculable for an MTurk pool. Self-report throughout. Multi-item scales with Cronbach's alpha 0.86-0.94, CR > 0.7, AVE > 0.6, HTMT < 0.85. Verification and correction each measured with a SINGLE item. Path model in SPSS Amos 26; CFI = 0.968, SRMR = 0.035. Author-stated limitations: MTurk validity debate, cross-sectional design cannot test causality, general rather than claim-specific behavioural measures. The 79.26% figure appears only in the sample description with no accompanying item wording, so it is not independently checkable.
rob.item6_quote: Often defined as false or inaccurate information, misinformation could inflame social conflicts (Valenzuela et al., 2019), decrease institutional trust (Kim and Cao, 2016), precipitate public health crises (WHO, 2020a), and inflict economic damage (Velichety and Shrivastava, 2022).
rob.item10_quote: The final sample consisted of 410 individuals ranging in age from 18 to 75 (M = 33.98, SD = 10.79). ... The majority (79.26 %) indicated that they often encountered news and information that contain misleading content.
